units.name: 91 Animal Behavior
units.passage: For much of the twentieth century, behaviorists assumed that animals learned only through conditioning and that, given enough training, any creature could be taught virtually any association or habit. Researchers today paint a very different picture. Although conditioning still plays a role, most animal learning turns out to be specialized for the particular tasks a species is likely to face in its life. An animal comes into the world already prepared to know when learning should happen, which signals deserve its attention, how fresh information ought to be stored, and how that information can be retrieved later. Even the more advanced invertebrates seem to rely on this kind of inborn direction, shaped by the needs of their own kind. Consider the chickadee. Despite its tiny brain, this little bird can recall where it has stashed hundreds of seeds, while a typical person starts losing track after hiding roughly twelve objects. Seen this way, every species, our own included, is clever in exactly those areas where natural selection rewarded cleverness and limited in the rest. This view ties the field of animal behavior together in a new way and promises fresh insight into where humans came from.

units.name: 92 Digital Technology
units.passage: Digital tools and online platforms are moving us away from a single mass culture toward a growing number of parallel cultures. Whether or not we notice it, each of us is a member of several different "tribes" at the same moment: we may share certain interests with the people we work with and quite different ones with our relatives. We even have things in common with strangers we have never seen in person and hardly think of as real individuals, such as the writers of blogs we follow or influencers on social media. Put simply, by giving us an enormous range of content to choose from, these technologies are also building new kinds of social structures. When a mass culture splits apart, it does not simply come back together as another large mass. Instead, it breaks into countless microcultures that exist side by side and interact with one another in unexpected ways. For this reason, culture is better understood not as one huge blanket that covers everyone but as a fabric of many overlapping threads woven together. Each thread can be reached on its own, and each one links several different groups of people at the same time.

units.name: 93 Classical Music
units.passage: By about 1900, audiences at classical concerts could no longer yell, snack, or chat while the musicians played, because the places where this music was performed had changed. The new rules were partly a means of keeping the lower classes, who were assumed to be naturally loud, away from the freshly built symphony halls and opera houses. Music that had often been enjoyed by everyone thus became the property of the wealthy few. Yet this policy of exclusion shaped the music itself as well. With listeners no longer talking, eating, or dancing, composers were free to use extreme contrasts between loud and soft. Since they could count on every small detail reaching the audience, they began to write extremely quiet sections, along with passages whose complex harmonies listeners could now properly appreciate. In fact, a great deal of classical music from the twentieth century was composed specifically for these socially and acoustically controlled halls and could succeed only there. In this way, a kind of music that had never existed before was born, and later, as recording technology appeared and improved, it became available almost everywhere.

units.name: 94 FOMO (Fear of Missing Out)
units.passage: Fear of Missing Out, or FOMO, is one of the defining psychological trends of our era, and it grows stronger whenever something seems to be in short supply. The mistake of overvaluing what is scarce is in fact extremely common. A friend of mine who sells real estate offers a good illustration. Whenever a potential buyer keeps hesitating, she phones him and mentions that a doctor from London came to look at the property the day before and was very impressed. Then she asks what he thinks. The doctor, who is sometimes replaced by a professor or a banker, does not actually exist. Still, the trick works remarkably well, and the buyer usually signs the contract. Viewed objectively, this makes little sense. A sensible decision about purchasing the land ought to depend only on how much the buyer really wants it and on the price being asked, not on invented tales about rival buyers. However, people rarely behave in a purely rational manner. The idea of scarcity makes the buyer feel that the chance is limited or about to disappear, and this feeling pushes him to act and complete the deal, even when doing so is not entirely logical.

units.name: 95 Astronomical Event
units.passage: Why does the transit of Venus, the rare event in which Venus travels directly between our planet and the Sun, matter so much? While a transit is under way, observers on Earth can spot Venus as a tiny dark dot gliding across the Sun's bright disk. Throughout history, however, this event has meant far more than just one celestial body passing in front of another. In 1639, the astronomer Jeremiah Horrocks used it to make the known universe much larger, though he had not set out to do so. He worked out the astronomical unit (AU), which is the distance between Earth and the Sun. To do this, he recorded how long Venus needed to cross the Sun as seen from two separate locations and then applied trigonometry to calculate how distant the Sun had to be. His result, 56 million miles, was nearly ten times larger than the figure scientists had previously accepted. Robert Walsh, an astrophysicist based at Central Lancashire University, has noted that this single number allowed Horrocks to enlarge the solar system. Later techniques, such as bouncing radio signals off the Sun's surface and measuring how long they take to come back, have proved more precise than Horrocks's approach, and today the AU is believed to be roughly 93 million miles.

units.name: 96 Exploring Prehistory
units.passage: Long ago, the world was a place of chaos and clutter, and then human beings appeared. In the beginning, prehistoric people were probably not much tidier than most other creatures. Over time, though, they slowly acquired the ability to sort mushrooms into those that were safe to eat and those that were poisonous, to keep their hunting areas clear of any human traces that might warn animals away, and to arrange rotating turns for keeping watch. Evidence from archaeological sites as old as 1.5 million years indicates that early humans set aside particular places to store their tools. By 20,000 BC, some hunter-gatherer groups even kept distinct zones for meals, cooking, throwing away waste, and pastimes like stone carving. Some anthropologists believe the Neanderthals vanished partly because they were less orderly than our own early ancestors. The Neanderthals, a human species that split from the line of Homo sapiens about 500,000 years ago, flourished in Europe for some 100,000 years, yet the sites they left behind are noticeably messier. It seems clear, then, that a preference for certain kinds of order must have given early humans an advantage in the struggle to survive.

units.name: 97 Plants’ Stomata
units.passage: Stomata are tiny pores on the surface of leaves through which plants exchange gases with the air. If the ground beneath a plant stayed wet at all times, the plant could simply keep these pores open day and night. Most plants, however, grow in places where the soil does not remain damp. For them, open stomata mean a steady escape of water vapor. To replace what is lost, the roots draw up whatever moisture the soil holds until the earth becomes dry, and the plant ends up short of water. When this shortage grows serious, the unbroken columns of water running through the plant's internal plumbing begin to snap, and the plant becomes dehydrated. Air bubbles then appear within its cells, so the leaves can no longer lift water from below. The situation resembles trying to drink through a straw that has a hole in its side: no matter how hard you suck, little liquid rises, and eventually the plant dies. Since photosynthesis is impossible without giving up some water to the atmosphere, plants must strike a careful balance. They hold their stomata open long enough to make as much food as they can, yet close them before the water loss becomes dangerous.

units.name: 98 Time Perception
units.passage: Much of what we call the passage of time actually depends on how we perceive it. For a young child, time crawls: when you go from your first birthday to your second, the number of days you have lived is multiplied by two. For an older adult, a year seems to fly by, because it is only a small addition to a long life. Paying close attention to time also seems to slow it almost to a stop, which is why people say that a watched pot never boils; the person staring at it loses patience because the wait feels endless. On the other hand, when we are not aware of time at all, as during sleep or during deeply rewarding moments of total concentration like those enjoyed by athletes, musicians, and writers, time stops mattering. Physics adds another layer to this complexity. According to Einstein's Theory of Relativity, time is not absolute or fixed but depends on one's position. Where gravity is stronger, closer to the Earth's surface, time runs more slowly. As a result, your feet actually age a tiny bit more slowly than your head! Time, then, can change with physical conditions, just as our sense of it changes with age and awareness.

units.name: 99 Paradigm Shift
units.passage: Philosophers of science have shown again and again that any single body of data can support more than one theoretical interpretation. The history of science also suggests that, especially while a new paradigm is still in its early stages, producing such rival explanations is not particularly hard. Even so, constructing alternatives is exactly what scientists rarely do, apart from the period before a paradigm has formed and a few exceptional moments later in a field's development. Why should this be so? As long as the instruments a paradigm provides keep succeeding at the puzzles that the paradigm itself sets, science advances most rapidly and explores most thoroughly when researchers rely on those instruments with confidence. Factories behave in much the same way: replacing equipment is costly, so it is done only when it truly cannot be avoided, and science follows this rule as well. This is why crises matter so much in science. A crisis is a signal that the existing tools have begun to fail and that the moment has finally come to retool.

units.name: 100 Cognitive Sharing
units.passage: Because of the way the brain builds representations of the world, a pair of people, a small group, or even a crowd of fifty can share roughly the same point of view. This shared cognition is what makes it so thrilling to listen to jazz, to watch improvised comedy, or to see players pass the ball among themselves, each predicting what the others will do to bring the ball close to the goal. To a certain extent, we go through what every other member of the audience goes through; and depending on how skilled and involved we are, we also partly feel what the performers themselves feel. The same sharing lets the members of a heart surgery team or a World Cup squad foresee each other's intentions and needs, work out problems, and react faster than any one person could manage alone. We are carried into a state of intense coordination and synchronization whose pace can outrun conscious thought. By sharing cognition in this way, we momentarily feel ourselves moving beyond the limits of the individual self.

units.name: 101 Aesthetic Sense
units.passage: One major reward of drawing is that it makes us consciously aware of why particular landscapes and buildings appeal to us. We start to account for our own preferences, and we gradually acquire an "aesthetic," that is, the ability to make confident judgments about what is beautiful and what is ugly. We become more precise in spotting what is missing from a building we dislike and what adds to the charm of one we admire. When we come across a striking view, we can quickly break it down and identify exactly where its force comes from. Instead of a vague "I like this," we learn to say "I like this because ...," and from there we move toward general ideas about what makes things pleasing. Although we may hold these ideas only tentatively and with some doubt, rules of beauty begin to suggest themselves: for example, light falling on objects from a street can create a feeling of space, and buildings should be no taller than the street is wide.

units.name: 102 Notable Journey of Money
units.passage: Money did not appear all at once. It developed slowly through a long chain of choices made by individual traders who were looking out for themselves and who knew only a limited amount about the market. At first, traders notice that when a direct swap, or barter, is hard to arrange, they can still get what they want by trading indirectly. They no longer have to search for a partner who both owns the thing they desire and desires the thing they own; it is enough to locate a person interested in what they are offering. They can accept that person's good even if they have no personal use for it, and later exchange it for something they really need. Here the good in the middle works as a medium of exchange. Sadly, goods are not all equally easy to trade, some selling far more readily than others. For this reason, traders are motivated to collect goods that are easy to sell and to employ them as media of exchange. Gradually, traders who see the benefits of sharing one medium of exchange settle on a single item, and that is how money comes into being.

units.name: 103 Multiculturalism
units.passage: For a long time, organizations dealt with cultural differences by asking people from minority backgrounds to fit in with the customs and expectations of the dominant group. Over roughly the last twenty years, however, campaigns to defend and expand minority rights have transformed the image of the workplace: once a "melting pot" in which differences dissolved, it is now pictured as a "salad bowl" in which each ingredient keeps its own character. Several forces explain this change in thinking. First, assimilation largely failed to deliver social justice, and that failure pushed people to look for fresh models. Second, civil rights legislation imposed legal duties that forced institutions to develop new methods of removing racial and gender bias from schools and hiring. Third, companies competing for an edge in the market have faced growing pressure to manage diversity by acknowledging cultural differences and working with them rather than against them. Globalization, which brings people of many cultures together, is now essential to competing strategically. After all, different cultural subgroups bring distinct attitudes toward work, ways of seeing, values, and norms, and these shape how well individuals and teams perform.

units.name: 104 Conventional Wisdom
units.passage: Back in the mid-1980s, some commentators predicted that as the United States moved from manufacturing toward services, most workers would end up stuck in poorly paid work such as flipping burgers or washing clothes. That forecast collapsed when the economy boomed during the 1990s. Likewise, the belief that Japan was about to surpass America as an economic power did not survive Japan's own decade of stagnation. Yet many other doubtful notions keep thriving, seemingly untouched by contrary facts or sound reasoning. This is not to say that all widely held beliefs are wrong; if they were, society could start to crumble as mistakes in everyday life piled up and spread disorder. Still, why are we so easily taken in by questionable ideas? The economist and public thinker John Kenneth Galbraith offered an explanation he called the inertia of beliefs. People hold tightly to what is familiar and comforting, and Galbraith traced this habit to an aversion to excessive originality. Such resistance, he suggested, is a practical compromise we make in order to get through ordinary life. If we questioned every belief and assumption all the time, we would be too paralyzed by doubt to decide anything.

units.name: 105 Paradox in Immunology
units.passage: Paradoxes tend to leave us feeling torn and unsure, largely because we have been trained to treat opposites, like curves and straight lines, as things that must stay apart. Yet when opposites overlap, they set up the conditions under which a fresh perspective can take shape in the mind. Louis Pasteur's discovery of the principle behind immunology came from exactly such a puzzle. He noticed that certain chickens which had earlier caught cholera managed to survive a second, more powerful infection, whereas chickens that had never been infected died. Pasteur understood that the survivors were, at one and the same time, sick and not sick: an earlier infection, too mild to be noticed, had kept them healthy and shielded them against the later attack. This seemingly contradictory notion, that a disease could serve to prevent disease, became the foundation of immunology as a science. In general, being able to picture opposing or conflicting ideas and images existing together in a single conceptual blend changes the way we think. It lets a kind of intelligence that goes beyond ordinary thought operate and produce something new.

units.name: 106 Adam Smith
units.passage: According to Adam Smith, every good has a natural price, one that mirrors the full amount of effort spent in producing it. This price is made up of three parts: the natural rent paid for land, the natural profit earned on capital, and the natural wage given for the labor involved. For a time, however, actual market prices and returns may move away from these natural levels, as can happen when goods become scarce. When this occurs, chances to make extra profit appear and prices go up, but only until market forces draw new businesses into the field, at which point prices drop back to their natural level. In much the same way, if demand for the products of one industry slumps, its prices sink and its wages decline, but as another industry grows, it raises wages to lure workers away. Smith argued that over the long term, market prices and natural prices end up identical. Today's economists refer to this state as equilibrium.

units.name: 107 Copyright
units.passage: Copyright exists to promote intellectual and artistic creativity. Paradoxically, though, granting creators excessive protection could end up holding back creative development instead of advancing it. To prevent this, copyright law protects only the specific language a writer uses to present facts and ideas; the facts and ideas themselves remain open for everyone to use. If an author were given exclusive control over the information and concepts found in a work, intellectual and artistic progress would be blocked rather than fostered. Consider what might have happened to science if Charles Darwin, after publishing On the Origin of Species, had been able to stop all other people from writing about evolution. Works whose value lies largely in the author's particular and distinctive wording, such as poems, novels, and plays, receive the strongest copyright protection. By contrast, factual works like histories, biographies, how-to guides, and news reports are given less protection, because the information they contain must remain available to all.

units.name: 108 Competitive Strategy
units.passage: People often think of manufacturing and services as two separate industries. In reality, however, manufacturers can build their competitive strategies around services, a process commonly called servitization. The term describes how manufacturing companies change so that they combine their traditional products with a full range of services, and firms can pursue it in different ways. Some makers just keep attaching more separate services to the goods they sell. Others work closely with a small number of key clients to create customized, personal arrangements that last for many years. Firms in this second group regard themselves as service providers and use their own skills in design and production to run and improve their customers' business processes. We call this second type advanced services. Such combinations of products and services require operations that are radically different from those of conventional manufacturing, yet when they are managed well, they contribute greatly to the manufacturer's long-term commercial survival.

units.name: 109 Cultural Orientation
units.passage: Scholars have not yet settled where individualism and collectivism, two contrasting cultural orientations, ultimately came from. One intriguing explanation, however, links these tendencies to how densely disease-causing microbes are concentrated in a region. According to this view, collectivist societies tend to flourish in parts of the world where infections are common. Collectivists generally feel greater suspicion toward strangers than individualists do, and they avoid the kinds of risky behavior that could help illness spread. Their wariness of outsiders protected them from unfamiliar germs against which their immune systems had no defense. Individualists, by contrast, were more willing to leave their own group and mix with foreigners, so when they came back from their journeys, they sometimes carried new infections home. As a result, individualistic cultures did best in regions where dangerous diseases were relatively rare. In such places, people could afford to be hardworking and adventurous, whereas collectivist peoples placed a higher value on group unity and harmony as a way of coping with threats from outside.

units.name: 110 Natural Selection
units.passage: The peppered moth owes its name to its speckled look: most members of the species are pale, with dark spots scattered across their wings. Observers were therefore puzzled when large numbers of entirely black moths began to appear in the population in some regions. In 1955, the British ecologist H.B.D. Kettlewell explained this striking shift. He observed that after the Industrial Revolution began, soot released by English factories built up on the trunks of trees and turned their bark a much deeper shade. The rise in the proportion of black moths, he concluded, resulted from the way pollution had altered the trees, a process now called industrial melanism. This process is a textbook case of natural selection. In clean woodlands, speckled moths enjoy an edge, since their pale coloring hides them against light bark. Black moths, in contrast, stand out clearly on such pale trunks, so birds catch and eat them more often. In polluted districts, however, the situation is turned upside down: dark moths are concealed by their coloring, while the speckled ones become easy to spot and are eaten in greater numbers.

units.name: 111 Motivations
units.passage: Researchers in social psychology increasingly stress that intrinsic motivations, such as a sense of moral duty or genuine curiosity about a task, differ from extrinsic ones, such as cash or other concrete rewards. If people take part in an activity because they believe it is valuable for its own sake, paying them may actually reduce their drive, because the money devalues or "crowds out" the inner interest or dedication they had. Conventional economic theory, in contrast, treats every motivation as simply a preference, regardless of its nature or origin, and supposes that motivations are additive; that is, they can be added together without changing one another. This assumption overlooks the way money can eat away at intrinsic motives. The crowding-out effect therefore matters greatly for economics. It raises doubts about relying on markets and market thinking in many areas of social life, such as using financial incentives to boost performance in schools, hospitals, workplaces, volunteer groups, and civic activities, where intrinsic motivations and moral commitments play an important role. As the economist Reto Jegen points out, if crowding out really occurs, offering more money could lower supply instead of raising it.

units.name: 112 Clocks
units.passage: The customs that grew up around the clock have profoundly shaped the way we understand time. That a day consists of twenty-four equal parts, each made up of sixty minutes, now seems a natural feature of everyday awareness. Beyond this, the clock offered fresh models for picturing the universe itself. In 1687, Isaac Newton released his Principia, a work in which he laid out his grand theories of how nature functions and where humanity stands in the cosmos. In this book, he pictured the universe as an enormous clock-like machine that runs with precision and predictability according to physical laws. This philosophical vision went on to influence the ideas that shape how people think and act every day. Notably, the clock was invented well before Newton developed his theories, and it strongly influenced the way he framed them. This shows that technological inventions can affect how scientists form and communicate their ideas.

units.name: 113 Social Transition
units.passage: In the earliest farming communities, growing food still took up most of people's effort, so the scope of their social contact stayed fairly limited. Later, when farmers began using draft animals to pull plows and carts, humans had to spend less of their own physical energy and gained more leisure time. This freedom allowed people to take part in a wider range of pursuits, and social structures grew more complicated. Eventually, water and wind came to be recognized as outstanding sources of energy. Rather than relying on animals, which had to be fed and looked after, people turned to waterwheels and windmills. Thanks to this shift, they could draw on more power than before, and it cost them less when measured in terms of human energy input. Consequently, society came to possess far more surplus energy than ever, and this abundance, in turn, encouraged progress in trade, transportation, and technology while also making human activities more diverse.

units.name: 114 Plasticity
units.passage: Brain plasticity can work in our favor when the continuous sensory input we take in is enjoyable, since it lets us build a brain that becomes better at noticing and relishing pleasant feelings. Yet the same plasticity can turn into a burden when the system receiving constant input is the one that handles pain. Long-lasting pain can reshape the brain so that, over time, the nerves react more strongly to pain signals. As a result, the pain grows sharper and more difficult to treat, even after the original injury has healed. Plasticity also affects bad habits, and it can give a person the chance to unlearn his or her own behavior. Imagine a man who has gotten into the habit of eating every time he feels emotionally troubled. In his mind, the enjoyment of food is tied to relief from emotional distress, so to break the habit, he must learn to separate the two. He may need to deliberately keep himself out of the kitchen whenever he is upset, until he discovers a healthier way of dealing with his feelings.

units.name: 115 Thought Experiments
units.passage: Since theoretical physics first emerged as a field, the thought experiment has served as one of its most valuable tools. Rather than building actual equipment, a scientist pictures an imaginary device and runs a simple test on it entirely within the mind, aiming to confirm or reject a particular hypothesis. A famous case is Galileo's argument against Aristotle, who had claimed that heavier bodies fall more quickly than lighter ones. Galileo showed instead that in a vacuum, objects of unequal mass fall with identical acceleration. Someone might assume that settling this question would require dropping real objects, but Galileo merely invited us to imagine two stones, one heavy and one light, joined by an extremely thin cord. If Aristotle's claim held, the lighter stone would act as a drag on the heavier one, while the heavier stone would pull the lighter one along, so the pair should descend more slowly than the heavy stone on its own. Yet by Aristotle's own logic, the joined pair, having a greater combined mass, ought to fall faster than either stone separately. Because the same theory predicts two contradictory outcomes, it cannot be correct. Galileo therefore concluded that every object, whatever its weight, falls through a vacuum at an equal rate.

units.name: 116 Ethnicity in Archaeology
units.passage: Beyond illuminating humanity's distant history, archaeology has helped scholars piece together the identities of cultural groups, trace where ethnic populations came from, and map how peoples moved across regions. In several nations, the discipline has become a wellspring of patriotic feeling. Greece, Egypt, and Italy are good examples, since their written histories and ancient ruins point to the splendor of once-mighty civilizations. Similar sentiments appear elsewhere: the French take pride in how their forebears stood up to the Roman invaders, Italians celebrate their descent from Rome, and Israelis turn to the archaeology of the Iron Age to back up claims about their history. Many archaeologists in Europe continue to assume that the objects they dig up belong to particular ethnic groups. In reality, however, assigning a clear ethnic identity to an ancient culture is difficult, because material culture tends to be borrowed, shared, and reshaped among neighboring peoples. This uncertainty, though, has not prevented politicians from exploiting archaeology to spread twisted versions of history that serve their own agendas. Sri Lanka offers a striking case. The two sides in its lengthy civil war each insisted that their people were the island's first settlers. Each refused to permit any excavation, worried that new findings might strengthen the opposing side's position.

units.name: 117 Legacy of Colonialism
units.passage: Over forty nations around the globe have no coastline at all. Fourteen of them lie in Africa, and their situation can be traced back to the colonial period. When European powers took control of much of the continent starting in the late nineteenth century, their main goal was to remove minerals and other raw goods from Africa's interior and carry them to the coast, where ships would transport them to Europe. To speed up this flow of resources, the colonizers built roads and railways that ran toward port cities. Once colonial rule came to an end, the new independent states inherited this economic infrastructure. Unfortunately, short of money and caught up in conflicts over borders, they were unable to keep it in good repair. Consequently, no former colony achieved complete regional development, and the inland territories were neglected more than any other area, which is why they now rank among the poorest places in Africa. On top of this, their hopes for future growth are limited because they have no easy way to reach the sea. They depend on nearby countries for the use of ports, which restricts how fully they can take part in international trade.

units.name: 118 Animal Communication
units.passage: Dolphins' capacity to learn new sounds and their talent for mimicry are likely connected, pointing to a communication system that is broadly adaptable and complex. Peter Tyack proposed one explanation for this adaptability. He recorded the whistles of Scotty and Spray, two captive dolphins kept together in a single tank, and found that each animal used a preferred whistle, known as its signature whistle, along with a second, less common one. Interestingly, the second whistle of each dolphin turned out to be the signature of its tankmate. In other words, the two dolphins regularly copied each other's signatures. Tyack argued that they did this to get each other's attention, much as if one were calling out, "Scotty, are you there?" rather than repeatedly announcing its own name. Using signatures this way clearly resembles the way people use names. Since such a system demands that each dolphin create a distinctive signature of its own and also be able to reproduce the signatures of others, it may help explain, at least in part, why dolphins need vocal learning and imitation.

units.name: 119 Business Globalization
units.passage: Globalization refuses to follow strict, fixed rules. Almost every general principle comes with so many clear exceptions that managers may be tempted to ignore management theory entirely and simply trust their instincts. Take marketing, for instance. It seems like precisely the kind of work that multinational brands ought to hand over to their local managers. Yet when one branch of a global brand ran a local advertising campaign containing images that many residents considered offensive, the result was a strong public backlash. Embarrassed, the company was forced to bring control back to headquarters so that such problems would not happen again. In the same way, supporters of globalization consistently advise firms to fill top positions with people from as many nations and backgrounds as they can. However, Iridium, a satellite-phone company, collapsed because its culturally diverse board proved impossible to manage. Its twenty-eight directors spoke several different languages, so board meetings resembled small United Nations sessions, with headsets offering translations in five languages. Clashes between cultures and misunderstandings occurred all the time.

units.name: 120 Self-Disclosure
units.passage: Although opening up to others has clear benefits, several strong forces often push you to stay hidden behind a private self. One is social custom: talking about yourself at length, or sharing your emotions and needs with people outside your family, is frequently seen as impolite. Another is fear. You may hold back because you worry about being rejected, becoming the subject of gossip, or being exploited by someone who learns too much. You may also wonder how others will judge you. If you admit to a single weakness, people might decide you are entirely bad; if you mention a strength, you could be labeled a show-off; and if you voice an opinion, you may be expected to act on it by voting, donating, or volunteering. Lastly, you might actually fear knowing yourself. On some level you sense that revealing yourself would deepen your self-understanding, yet you also suspect that this process could uncover uncomfortable truths about your own character that you would prefer to keep out of sight.
